Therefore, thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will visit them. The young men shall die by the sword; their sons and daughters shall die by famine, and there shall be no remnant of them. For I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth in the year of their visitation. It seems that this contradicts the previous opinions, in which we wanted to approve what was said from the person of Christ, and not from Jeremiah, who resided in the village of Anathoth, which is three miles from Jerusalem. But if we understand the etymology of the town of Anathoth (which means obedience), it will clearly show that the men of Anathoth, who once obeyed the Lord's commands, were all called Jews, and especially the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, upon whom the final judgment came, that they would perish in the evils of the siege, by sword, famine, and disease. In order to free ourselves from all the annoyance of interpretation, let us follow this rule: Whatever the prophets have done in the manner of the Lord and Savior, and whatever has been fulfilled in the present time in Jeremiah, let it be prophesied in the future about the Lord.

n: Is just. Hebrew, "judgment." Septuagint, "I will make my apology to thee." Jeremias had been grievously persecuted by his countrymen: he therefore mentions a subject which has been the source of much perplexity. The success of the wicked is a temptation for weak souls. See Job xxi., Psalm lxxii. 3., and Habacuc i. 13. (Calmet) --- The prophets often speak in their names, not being ignorant or doubtful of the justice of divine providence. (Worthington)
Reins. They have thy name in their mouth, but not in their heart, Isaias xxix. 13., and Matthew xv. 8.
Gather. God orders his prophet to announce the misery of the wicked.

Mourn? Is not this a proof of my providence in chastising Juda? This famine is specified [in] chap. viii. 13., and xiv. 4. (Calmet) --- Last end. Two letters seem to be transposed in Hebrew, as the Septuagint read "ways." (Kennicott) --- The impious blaspheme as if all were ruled by chance. (Calmet)

Horses. If thou hast been terrified at the threats of thy fellow-citizens, how wilt thou withstand those of Jerusalem? (Menochius) or he speaks to Juda, who would not be able to resist the Chaldeans, since the Philistines, &c., had routed the Jews, though destitute of cavalry. --- Jordan, or the nations of Ammon, &c., on that side. (Calmet) --- Protestants, "if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt," &c. (Haydock)
To thee. Edom, &c., made a league with Sedecias, which they broke. They always bore a hatred to the Jews, though sprung from the same stock, chap. xxvii. 1., and Lamentations iv. 21. (Calmet)
Soul; people, (Haydock) whose punishment was decreed. Say not, therefore, that the wicked always prosper.

As a. Septuagint, "a den of the hyena:" Alexandrian, "robbers." Grabe inserts, "or a den around it?" (Haydock) --- They have read áuss, "a den," instead of hait, "a bird." Bochart, (iii. 11.) however, shews that the latter word denotes various wild beasts, and nearly follows the Septuagint. Though the inheritance be most charming, it shall not pass unpunished. (Calmet)
Pastors; princes of my people, as well (Haydock) as of the Chaldeans, chap. vi. 3.
Heart, to seek God and the cause of their misfortunes.
Fruits. They shall not satisfy your expectations or wants.
Land. Nabuchodonosor led the Ammonites, &c., into captivity, five years after the Jews. (Josephus, Antiquities x. 11.) (Calmet) --- After the children are chastised, the rod is burnt. (Worthington)
Land; the Jews, as well as their neighbours, chap. xlix. 6. (Menochius) (Isaias xxiii. 15., and Ezechiel xvi. 55.)
People. After the captivity, converts were more cherished. Yet the predictions concerning the call of the Gentiles were accomplished only by the preaching of the gospel. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 10

"You are righteous, Lord, that I shall make my defense before you. Yet I will speak judgments to you. Why is it that the way of the ungodly prospers? All those who deal treacherously in treacheries have flourished." We still inquire whether God, who has given the Law and the Prophets, is good, seeing that "the way of the ungodly prospers" and he does not punish the ungodly. "All those who deal treacherously in treacheries have flourished." Those very ones who speak against the Creator, who blaspheme him, "have flourished, they have been planted and rooted, they have begotten children and have produced fruit." How much fruit has Marcion produced by begetting children, how much Basilides, how much Valentinus? For this is what is prophesied concerning the ungodly and said in the words "they have begotten children and produced fruit." "You are near to their mouth, but far from their reins": they name the name of Jesus, but they do not have Jesus; for they do not confess him as they ought.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Chapter 12 - Verses 1 onwards) Indeed, you are just, O Lord, if I argue with you (or because I want to satisfy you); however, I will speak to you about judgments. What is it that the way of the wicked prospers? It is well for all who break the law and act unjustly. You have planted them and they have taken root, they grow and bear fruit (or they have borne children and produce offspring). You are near their mouths, but far from their hearts. Truly, this is a discussion of all those who act unjustly, and the meaning is summarised in the 72nd Psalm, in which the Prophet says: How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart! But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious of the wicked, seeing the prosperity of sinners, etc. (Psalm 73:1-2). However, this is especially said against heretics, who, though they are impious, prosper in their ways; and they beget children whom they have deceived in their heresy, and they act deceitfully and unjustly, so as to rob the Church. And while they persist in their wickedness of opinion, they boast that they are planted by God, and that they have sent forth roots, and have begotten children and brought forth fruit. But although they often repeat the name of Christ, they do not have God as their dweller, according to that of Isaiah: This people honors me with their lips: but their heart is far from me (Isaiah 29:13).
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 10

"And you, Lord, know me, you have seen me, you have tested my heart before you; purify them for the day of their slaughter." What shall I do, that I may make these things clear? He calls the punishments a purification of those being punished; for "purify them," he says, "for the day of their slaughter." Through their being slaughtered, purify them; for "whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives."
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 3.) And you, Lord, you know me: you have seen me, and you have tested my heart with you. Gather them together like a flock for the sacrifice, and sanctify them on the day of slaughter. There is no scandal, it is said, that the wicked, or all heretics, flourish for a time: For you, Lord, know me, and you have seen me, and you have tested my heart with you. How does the Father God know his Son this way? For no one knows the Son except the Father: and no one knows the Father, except the Son, and whom the Son wants to reveal (Matt. XI, 17). It is permitted, he says, that they may prosper, that they may generate children, and that heretics may produce fruit, and you may be close to their mouth and far from their kidneys, that is, their conscience: nevertheless, there is some consolation, in that they are fattened like sheep for the slaughter. Gather them in the city of Jerusalem, or in their assemblies: so that they may be slaughtered as if they were victims of death, and then may be sanctified, when they have been beheaded by the sword of the Church: for the killing of heretics is the salvation of those who had been deceived.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 10

"How long shall the land mourn and the grass of the field be dried up from the wickedness of those who dwell in it?" As though of a land that has a soul, here too the prophet discourses, saying that the land mourns because of the wickedness of those who tread upon it. In the case of each one of us, then, the land either mourns or rejoices; for it either mourns "from the wickedness of those who dwell in it," or it rejoices from the virtue of those who dwell in it. In the case of each one of us, then, the very element either rejoices or mourns. And if the land, then perhaps the remaining elements too. I will say likewise both the water and the angel appointed over the water, that I may explain also the land that mourns or does not mourn; for it is not this body, "the land," that mourns "from those who dwell in it," but understand for me that, in addition to the ordering of the whole, a certain angel is appointed over the land, and another appointed over the waters, and another over the air, and a fourth over the fire. Thus ascend for me by reasoning to the whole ordering that is in animals, that is in plants, that is in the heavenly stars. A certain angel is appointed both over the sun, and another over the moon, and another also over the stars; these angels, then, with whom we are — insofar as we are of earth — either rejoice if we act righteously, or mourn over us when we sin. The land mourns, he says, from those who dwell in it. By homonymy he called the angel "land" with the very land itself. For just as "the handmade thing is accursed, both it and the one who made it" — not that the lifeless thing itself is accursed, but that which sits beside the lifeless image and passes under that name is called "handmade" — so also I will say that the angel appointed over land is called "land," and the angel appointed over water is called "water," according to what has been said: "The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid, the depths were troubled by the multitude of the sound of the waters, the clouds gave a voice, for indeed your arrows pass through."
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 4) How long will the earth mourn, and all the herbage of the region wither because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it? The animal and the bird have perished because they have said: Our last things will not be seen (or God will not see our ways). Whatever happens in the world, whether good or evil, happens not without the providence and chance of God, but by his judgment. The earth is now barren, the herbage dries up. Do you want to know the reason? Those who dwell in wickedness do this: so that the animals on the earth and the birds of the sky are consumed, because all these creatures were created for the use of humans: who have risen to such blasphemy as to say that God is ignorant of His own ways, and does not know what each individual will suffer. But what he says, 'How long?' signifies the enduring wrath of God, because the hearts of sinners were not inclined to repentance.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 5) If you have struggled running with foot soldiers, how will you be able to compete with horses? If you have relied on the land of peace, what will you do in the pride or tumult of the Jordan? If, as they say, you have been wearied by the frequent captivities of neighboring nations, the Moabites and Ammonites, the Philistines and Edomites, what will you do in the face of a long captivity that will be led by the Chaldeans all the way? And he compares foot soldiers to horsemen, for in truth both the Persians and the entire Chaldean empire and the armies of those regions take delight in cavalry according to history. But these nations, which I mentioned above, are not so suited for battle because of the difficulty of the terrain, as they are for robbery. And he preserves the metaphor and says: If you became weak with fatigue while running alongside foot soldiers, what will you do if you want to keep up with horses? And if you had any confidence in your own land, what will you do when you cross the Jordan and endure its currents?
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 6.) For even your brothers and the household of your father themselves fought against you, and they cried out after you with a loud voice: do not believe them when they speak good things to you. To such an extent, he says, you will be overwhelmed by the most violent waves of the Jordan, and the multitude of horsemen coming from afar will devastate you, so that even your brothers from the Edomite lineage, and the household of your father, who are descendants of Lot, Moab and Ammon, themselves will fight against you in times of necessity and distress, and will insult you (Genesis 19). Beware of trusting them and having hope in kinship, through which they may rage against you more than your enemies. This can also be understood in reference to Jesus, that his brothers and the household of his father fought against him and cried out loudly, saying: Crucify him, crucify him: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15).
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 10

"I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies." Behold for me the one who exists "in the form of God," being in the heavens; behold his house, above the heavens. And if you wish to see something yet higher (that he is "in the Father"), behold that his house is God. He leaves "the father and the mother," the "Jerusalem above," and comes to the earthly place and says, "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance." For that was his inheritance, the regions with the angels, the rank with the holy powers. "I have given my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies." He delivered his soul into the hands of the enemies of the soul, into the hands of the Jews who killed him, into the hands of the rulers gathered together against him, into the hands of kings, when "the kings of the earth stood by and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ."
Letter 75.3, 5

And although the Apostle himself told the Hebrews that a testament is of no force, until the death of the testator happen, that is to say, a testament is of no strength while the testator liveth, but is established by his death, yet as in Jeremiah the Lord, speaking of the Jews, has said, Mine heritage is unto Me as a lion, he would not deny that they were heirs. But there are heirs without possessions, there are heirs also with them; and while the testator lives those whose names are written in the will are called heirs, though without possessions... As then young children, so the Jews also, are under a schoolmaster. The Law is our schoolmaster, the schoolmaster brings us to our Master; and our One Master is Christ: Neither be ye called masters, for one is your Master, even Christ.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Vers. 7, 8.) I left my house, I abandoned my inheritance: I gave my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies. My inheritance became like a lion in the forest: it roared against me, therefore I hated it. He who spoke in the Gospel: Rise, let us go from here (John 14:31). And again: Your house will be left desolate (Luke 13:35), here and also in the same prophet he threatens; and he says that he has done what he was going to do. For the inheritance of the Lord is Israel, and his inheritance is as a rope. But when he says: 'I have given my beloved soul into the hand of his enemies,' that means, I have the power to lay down my soul, and I have the power to take it up again (John 10:18). Indeed, the inheritance of the Lord, the people of the Jews, once rebelled against him like a lion in the forest: when they shouted with a loud voice against him in their suffering. And because they raised their voice against him, he therefore hated them, and rejected them, and what was once beloved and cherished is now called hateful.
Commentary on Matthew

Behold, your house will be left to you deserted. He had said this very thing long before, in the person of Jeremiah: I have left my house, I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like the cave of a hyena. We prove that the house of the Jews, that is, that temple which before shone more majestically to the eyes, is deserted, because it lost Christ its inhabitant and, eager to snatch the inheritance, killed the heir.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 10

"My inheritance became to me as a lion in a thicket." This inheritance of his upon the earth, which he had received as inheritance, turned savage against him, and the inheritance — the Jews — became wild against him "as a lion in a thicket." It is no wonder if then his inheritance became "as a lion in a thicket"; even now there are still lions in the thicket wishing to curse Jesus and blaspheming him and plotting against those who believe in him. "My inheritance," then, "became to me as a lion in a thicket. It uttered its voice against me; therefore I hated it."
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 10

"Is my inheritance to me a hyena's den?" He prophesies concerning this inheritance: has my inheritance perhaps become a hyena's den, a hyena's den — of the most savage beast, the corpse-eater, the one about the tombs, the one that eats the dead bodies? "Is my inheritance to me a hyena's den? Or a cave round about it on every side? Go." Since they have become such, I command you, the angels, to go and gather the beasts and deliver them to the beasts. "Go and gather all the beasts of the field, and let them come to devour it." The beasts of the field have come; they devour that people. See their hearts being devoured by the opposing powers. If Jesus did not spare those, but said, "Go, gather the beasts," how much more will he not spare us? If we do not do the Law of God, the word of the Gospel, he will say again: Go, gather the beasts and deliver it up. But we have boldness to say in our prayers: "Do not deliver to the beasts a soul that confesses to you." Let us confess concerning our transgressions, repenting, and we shall not be delivered to the beasts, but to holy angels who will be nurses, bearing us upon their bosoms, transferring us from this age to the age to come in Christ Jesus, to whom is the power and the glory unto the ages. Amen.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Ver. 9.) Is my inheritance like a colorful bird to me? Is it like a bird dyed all over? Come, gather all the beasts of the earth; hurry to devour. LXX: Is the den of the hyena my inheritance? Is there a den all around it, above it? Go, gather all the animals of the field; let them come and eat it. According to the letter, he calls the colorful and fully dyed bird a peacock. He says that Israel had such great beauty and Jerusalem was distinguished by such virtues that there was nothing good that could not be seen in it. Therefore, since an inheritance was once made for me, that is, the people of Israel, like a lion in the forest, and they spoke against me, and I detested them with all hatred: therefore come and gather against them all the beasts of the earth, a multitude of diverse nations, and devour them who have not known their Lord. But if, as the Septuagint and other interpreters have translated, it is read: Is my inheritance to me a den of hyenas, shall we return to the uncleanness of the nocturnal beast, which lives on the corpses of the dead, and is accustomed to dig up bodies from tombs, and there is no filthiness that it does not feed on. Such is Israel offending his Lord, and delivered to the bites of all beasts.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 10) Many shepherds have destroyed (or disrupted) my vineyard, they have trampled (or polluted) my portion: they have given my desirable portion into a desert wasteland (or uninhabited). They have made (or it has been made) it into a desolation. Let those who want to be leaders of the people hear this, because they will have to give an account not only for themselves, but also for the flocks entrusted to them, on the day of judgment. For because of them, a part of the Lord's dwelling place is trampled and polluted, so that where once there was a hospice, there may now be a dwelling place for beasts. Others, however, understand the leaders of the enemies, who have scattered the vineyard of the Lord, not as being placed over the people and priests.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 11

Who is it that says, "Because of me the whole earth has been laid utterly waste"? Christ says these things, before whose coming many sins had indeed been committed by the people, but not such sins as to cause them to be utterly forsaken and handed over into a captivity of long duration. But when they had filled up "the measure of their fathers" and had added, to the killing of the prophets and the persecuting of the righteous, the slaying of "the Christ of God," then came to pass the word, "Your house is left to you." And it is because of him that they have suffered these things, and "the whole earth has been laid utterly waste."

But if you wish also to hear in a loftier sense the words, "Because of me the whole earth has been laid utterly waste," look at the earth within you, in what manner it was laid waste when Jesus came; for it was laid waste "when the members that are upon the earth were put to death," and the earth no longer works its own works, no longer are there produced in the righteous person the works of the flesh in which the flesh once flourished — no longer fornication, no longer uncleanness, not licentiousness, not idolatry, not sorcery, and the rest. And the Savior too says, "Do you think that I came to cast peace upon the earth? I did not come to cast peace, but a sword." For truly, before he came, there was no sword upon the earth, nor did "the flesh lust against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh"; but when he came and we were taught which things are of the flesh and which are of the spirit, the teaching, having become as it were a sword upon the earth, divided the flesh and the earth from the spirit; and "the earth was laid waste" when we carry about the dying of Jesus in the body, and we no longer live according to the flesh but the spirit lives, and we sow nothing unto the flesh but all things unto the spirit, so that we may not reap corruption from the flesh but from the spirit eternal life.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Vers. 11, 12.) And the earth mourned, desolate it is, because there is no one who thinks in their heart. The devastators have come over all the paths of the desert, for the sword of the Lord has devoured from one end of the earth to the other: there is no peace for all flesh. LXX: Therefore the earth is utterly ruined, and the rest. This that we have set, 'and the earth mourned,' is joined to the previous verse according to the Hebrew, so that the meaning is: They have made it into ruin, that is, my inheritance: And the earth mourned, deprived of my help. But according to the Septuagint, God spoke that because of him the earth is devastated and turned into a wilderness, because there is no one who remembers in their heart, nor any peace for all flesh. For the flesh cannot receive the peace of God. For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God. And according to the Hebrew, therefore all of Judaea is desolate, because there is no one who remembers God in their heart, nor is there any survivor who can escape. For through all the ways of solitude came the devastators, that is, a hostile army, and the sword of the Lord devoured from one end to the other; and there was no rest for those fleeing from the city. Hence it is said: There is no peace for all flesh.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 11

And it is said to those who have sinned, "You sow wheat and you reap thorns"; for even if they discourse in the oracles of God, those who do not discourse rightly in them, nor live in the way they ought, nor believe, are sowing wheat and reaping thorns. And these things are most of all to be understood with reference to the heterodox, who engage with the Scriptures and reap thorns not from the Scriptures but from their own inventions. "Their lots will not profit them." These things others also have expounded. And since we do not reject their exposition, we in good conscience bring it forward into the midst, not as though we had found it ourselves, but as having learned a good lesson. This word will profit both you and us, if we attend to what is written — we who seem to be certain persons appointed from the clergy and set over you, so that some desire to come to this clerical order. But know that the clerical order does not by any means save; for many even among the presbyters will perish, and many even among the laity will be shown to be blessed. Since, then, there are some in the clergy who do not live in such a way as to be profited and to adorn the clerical order, for this reason, say those who have expounded, it is written, "Their lots will not profit them." For that which profits is not the mere sitting in the presbytery, but the living worthily of the place, as the word demands. The word demands that both you live well and we. But, if it must be so put, "the mighty shall be mightily tested"; more is demanded of me than of the deacon, more of the deacon than of the layman, and he to whom has been entrusted the rule over all of us, the very rule of the Church, is required to give account still more. For this reason the apostle, to whom the great things have been entrusted, listen, says: "Let a man so account of us, as of ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here, moreover, it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful." And so it is a rare thing to be found a faithful and good steward. Jesus, "who knows all things before their coming to be," says, "Who then is the faithful and prudent steward, whom his lord shall set over his household, to give them their measure of grain in due season?" Then he blames certain stewards and says, "But if the wicked servant begin to say, My lord delays his coming, and begin to beat his fellow-servants and the maidservants, and to eat and drink and be drunken, the lord of that servant shall come in a day when he does not expect and in an hour that he does not know, and shall cut him in two, and shall appoint his portion with the unbelievers." So much, then, for the words "Their lots will not profit them."

But let us look also at what follows, a necessary rebuke, which it is good to take up under the moral head, saying, "Be ashamed of your boasting, of the reproach before the Lord." There are certain things in which, through folly, we boast, though they are not worthy of boasting. For instance, if someone boast that he is rich and has acquired much, it may be said to him, "Be ashamed of your boasting." If someone boast in this outward nobility, it will be said to him, "Be ashamed of your boasting." If someone boast in the costliness of garments, in the building of a richly furnished house, such boasting is foreign to the boasting of the saints; therefore it will be said to such a one, "Be ashamed of your boasting." Hear the word of the prophet Jeremiah bidding us not to boast, not even in wisdom; for "let not," he says, "the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches, but let him that boasts boast in this, to understand and to know that I am the Lord." Do you wish to boast, and while boasting not to hear, "Be ashamed of your boasting"? Boast as the apostle does, and say, "But far be it from me to boast, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." Do you wish to boast, so that it may not be said, "Be ashamed of your boasting"? Listen to Paul boasting, and learn when he says, "Most gladly, therefore, will I boast in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest upon me." Hear what boastings he boasts: "in labors more abundantly" (which of us can say this?), "in prisons more exceedingly, in deaths often. Of the Jews five times I received forty stripes save one, thrice I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck." We learn, then, that there are also differences among boastings, in that some boastings are worthy of shame, of which that apostolic saying might be spoken, "and their glory is in their shame"; for in the things whereof they ought to be ashamed, in these they think to be glorified.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 13) They sowed wheat and harvested thorns: they received an inheritance, but it will not benefit them. LXX: You have sown wheat and harvested thorns: their clergy will not benefit them. They expected better things, but the worst came: they hoped for success, but endured adversity: they received an abundance of all things from the Lord, which will not benefit them. According to the Septuagint, all heretics sow wheat and harvest thorns, while the Lord waits for them to bear fruit, but they do not bring forth judgment, only outcry. But it is said also of Ecclesiastics who scatter the words of the Lord and his doctrine by evil conduct. Concerning them it is inferred: Their clergy shall not profit them. For what can bishops' name and presbyters, or the rest of the Ecclesiastical order, do to help them, when they are burdened more by their own dignities and suffer powerful torments severely, and when more has been entrusted to them, more is required of them (Wisdom 6).
LETTER 52.5

I beg you, therefore, and admonish you again and again: do not look to your military experience for a standard of clerical obligation. Under Christ's banner, do not seek worldly gain, lest having more than when you first became a clergyman, you hear people say, to your shame, "Their portion shall not profit them." Welcome poor people and strangers to your homely table, that with them Christ may be your guest.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Vers. 14, 15.) You shall be confounded by your fruits (or by your boasting (because of the anger of the fury of the Lord (or by the reproach in the sight of the Lord). Thus says the Lord against all my wicked neighbors, who touch the inheritance which I have distributed to my people Israel: Behold, I will uproot them from their land and uproot the house of Judah (or cast them out) from among them. And when I have uprooted them, I will turn (or return) and have mercy on them, and I will bring them back (or make them dwell) man in his inheritance, and man in his land. It is said to them, to whom their own clergy and ecclesiastical order will not benefit, that they should be confounded by their own boasting and by reproach before the Lord. And it brings forth: against all my wicked neighbors, according to the letter, the neighbors of the holy land are the Edomites, Philistines, Moab, and Ammon. But according to the allegory, all heretics who are considered under the name of Christ are even more neighbors than the inhabitants of the holy land, who touch the inheritance of God and devastate it. And it is said of them that they shall be taken away from the midst of the land, and the house of Judah shall be taken away from their midst. Whoever is uprooted and freed from the jaws of the heretics will obtain the mercy of God, and they will be restored to their inheritance and their land.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 16, 17.) And it shall come to pass, if the learned ones have learned the ways of my people, to swear in my name, as the Lord lives: just as they taught my people to swear by Baal, they shall be built up in the midst of my people. But if they do not listen, I will uproot that nation with destruction and annihilation, says the Lord. If those who have been translated from heresy into the Church have learned the ways of the people of God, and have sworn in the name of the Lord, and not in the name of the idols they themselves imagined, they shall be built up by the Lord, and they shall be a part of his people. But if those who have been translated into the Church hold on to the remnants of perverse doctrines and do not heed the words of the Lord, that people shall be uprooted from the midst of God's people, through perpetual destruction and removal, so that not a single place of repentance is left for them. We see this happening every day, and we have evidence that heretics, in order to deceive the simple-minded, pretend to uphold the truth of the faith, not so that they themselves may convert to the faith, but rather to lead the faithful into disbelief.

n: Girdle, usually worn by women. (St. Jerome) (Exodus xxviii. 42.) --- It denoted the Jews, who became more corrupt during the captivity; (ver. 7, 11.) so that God delivered them out of his pure mercy. Thus He explains this prophetical action. (Calmet) --- Loins. God cherished his people. (Menochius) --- Water. He made choice of them when they were rough and deformed. (St. Jerome) --- Their sins cause their ruin. (Haydock)

Euphrates, above 150 leagues distant. Some think this was only to be done in spirit: but it is generally supposed that the prophet made this long journey twice. Bochart suggests that Euphrates (Hebrew Peratha) may be put for Ephrata, or Bethlehem, as the first syllable is often cut off. (Calmet) --- Yet a journey to the Euphrates would represent more strikingly the destination of the people; and it would not be difficult for God to convey Jeremias thither in a short time, if requisite, as he sent Habacuc through the air to carry a dinner to Daniel; (xiv. 32.) though this supposition is not here necessary, as the labour to which Jeremias was repeatedly exposed, might shew the people their manifold transgressions and captivities. (Haydock) --- Such prophetic actions make a deeper impression than words, Hebrews i. The ingratitude of the people is here described, to chap. xxi. (Worthington)
Rot. I will bring them low. (Menochius) --- They shall see that all their dependance must be on the divine mercy.
Glory; that they might serve me for the edification of the world.

Bottle, of earthen ware, chap. xxv. 27. (Calmet) --- Every man shall suffer, ver. 13. (Haydock) --- This is another prophetical similitude denoting extreme perplexity. (Worthington) --- Do. They deride the prophet, as if he said nothing worthy of notice. (Menochius)
Dark. John xii. 35. --- Mountains, beyond the Euphrates, resembling clouds.
My soul. Jeremias can do no more. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "your soul,...your eyes," &c. (Haydock)
Queen; Nohesta, mother of Joachim, or to the consort of Sedecias. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "to the princes." (Haydock)
South, belonging to Juda; (Calmet) or Egypt will afford no protection. (Tournemine) (Chap. xxxvii. 3, 10.)
North: ye Chaldeans. (Haydock) --- Hebrew and Septuagint, "see those who come." --- Cattle. O king, what account wilt thou give of the people to the Almighty? (Calmet)
Head. Achaz called the Assyrians into the country, and Ezechias had shewn his treasures to the Babylonians. Other kings excited God's indignation.
Defiled. Thou art exposed to the brutality of the soldiers.
Evil. Bad habits are a sort of second nature. I speak in vain. (Calmet) --- Yet God sometimes converts inveterate sinners, who cannot rise of themselves. (Worthington)
Appeared. Thou art treated as a wretched and vile captive. (Haydock)
Me; to serve me. (Menochius)

f: The Stromata Book 3

Furthermore, this Paul said strongly that "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking"—or abstinence from wine or meat—"but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." Which of them goes around like Elijah wearing a sheepskin and a leather belt? Which of them wears no shoes and nothing but a piece of sackcloth like Isaiah? Or with nothing on but a linen loincloth, like Jeremiah?
The Instructor Book 2

The blessed John disdained sheep's wool because it savored of luxury; he preferred camel's hair and clothed himself in it, giving us an example of simple, frugal living. Incidentally, he also ate only honey and locusts, food that is sweet and with a spiritual significance. So it was that he prepared the way of the Lord and kept it humble and chaste. He fled from the false pretenses of the city and led a peaceful life in the desert with God, away from all vanity, boasting and servitude. How could he possibly have worn a purple mantle? Elijah used a sheepskin for his garment and girded it tight with a belt made of leather. Isaiah, another historic prophet, went "naked and without sandals" and often put on sackcloth as a garment of humility. If you protest and make mention of Jeremiah, he wore only a loincloth made of linen.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 11

After these things let us look at what concerns the loincloth. For "Thus," it says, "says the Lord: Go and acquire for yourself a linen loincloth, and put it around your loins, and do not pass it through water. And I acquired a loincloth according to the word of the Lord and put it around my loins. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Take the loincloth that is around your loins, and arise and go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in the cleft of the rock." After some days he comes there, and finds this loincloth rotted through. And the Lord adds to it, giving the occasion for the interpretation of the loincloth, saying: "Just as the loincloth clings to the loins of a man, so did I cause the house of Israel and the whole house of Judah to cling to myself, says the Lord, that they might become for me a renowned people and a boast and a glory, and they did not listen to me." Therefore the prophet is taken up in the place of God, girding around his loins the linen loincloth, as God girds the people; for "I caused to cling to myself," he says, "this people," meaning that the people, as it were, becomes God's loincloth.

But why does the people become God's loincloth around his loins? Let him who is able, reading Ezekiel and beholding God, as it were, given a bodily form by the word — and in what manner the parts of him from the loins downward are fire, but the parts from the loins upward are amber — let him search out the word, why the lower part of God is fire. The things from the loins and from generation, these are fire. For all things that are in generation have need of the purification that comes from fire, all things in generation have need of chastisement. But the things above the loins and beyond generation, these are matter as in its purest and most precious state; for amber is said to be more precious than gold. Since, then, the Scripture uses these figures, that it may teach that the upper body of God is more precious and the lower body more inferior, for this reason it introduced God as composed of fire and amber. Each of us is fire while in generation; we are not the amber; but if we ascend and make progress (for it is possible to pass from being today among the lower parts, so as to become the upper body of God), then, having passed through the fire, we shall be amber, the amber about the higher body of God. He clings, then, around his loins, the linen loincloth. To what end? That it may be shown that the people is, as it were, a covering of God; for against those who wish to accuse God the people stands, and as it were shields him and does not permit anything absurd to be said in matters concerning God. But when we sin, then, just as the prophet lays aside this loincloth and condemns it to the river Euphrates that it may there be destroyed, so the sinner is cast off from the loins of God and, being cast out, is cast out into the river Euphrates, the river of Mesopotamia, where the Assyrians are enemies to Israel, where the Babylonians are, and there he is destroyed. For though there are so many rivers, the prophet is sent from Judea to the river Euphrates to transact this business and to carry away a little linen loincloth.

But why also "linen"? Because it has its origin from the earth; for it is a plant springing up from the earth, then, after being cultivated, carded and washed and scoured and worked much, that it may become such as to become a loincloth or whatever else. And we too, then, all of us have our origin as the loincloth of God, and having our origin from the earth, we have need of much working, that we may be carded, that we may be washed, that we may cast off the color of the earth; for one is the color of the linen at its origin, another that which comes from the working. For the color of the linen at its origin is rather black, but from the working it becomes most brilliant. Some such thing, then, comes upon us also who are in generation. We are black at the beginning of our believing, wherefore at the beginning of the Song of Songs it is said, "I am black and beautiful." And at the beginning we resemble Ethiopians in the soul. Then we are scoured, that we may become more brilliant, according to the words, "Who is this that comes up made white?" And we become "brilliant and clean linen"; then also we are woven into the loincloth of God, when we are worthy to cling to God. God does not lay us aside. He laid aside the first people, "the whole house of Judah" and "the house of Israel." It came to be no longer used; for he no longer girds himself with them. In their place God girded himself with us; for he did not, having cast off the loincloth, remain naked, but wove for himself another loincloth. This loincloth is the Church that is from the nations; and let it know that "if God did not spare the former ones, how much more will he not spare it either when it sins," unless it be worthy of the loins of God; "but he that clings to the Lord is one spirit" in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Chapter 13, verse 1 onwards) Thus says the Lord to me: Go and acquire for yourself a linen loincloth (or belt) and put it on your loins, and do not bring it into water (or do not pass it through water). So I acquired a loincloth according to the word of the Lord and put it around my loins. Then the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: Take the loincloth (or belt) that you acquired, which is around your loins, and go to the Euphrates and hide it there in a hole in the rock. And I went and hid it in the Euphrates, as the Lord had commanded me. And after many days, the Lord said to me: Arise and go to the Euphrates, and take from there the girdle (or belt) that I commanded you to hide there. And I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and took the girdle from the place where I had hidden it, and behold, the girdle had decayed so that it was of no use. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord: So will I cause the pride (or injury) of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem and this evil people, who refuse to hear my words and walk in the stubbornness (or direction) of their evil hearts: they have gone after foreign gods to serve them and worship them, and they will be like this useless girdle. For as the waist is joined to the loins of a man, so have I joined to me all the house of Israel, and all the house of Juda, saith the Lord: that they might be my people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear. The girdle, or waistband, which is joined to the loins, is the people of Israel: they who have been taken up from the earth, and have not been softened, nor made white, and yet they have cleaved to God through his mercy. And when he sinned, because linen and a linen apron made of such material is rational, he was led across the Euphrates, that is, into Assyria, and there he was hidden, that is, absorbed in a multitude (or rather, magnitude) of great and innumerable nations, and regarded as nothing. But after a long time, the Prophet himself, as a type of God, freed the people from captivity. However, even after their return, they did not keep God's commandments; but they followed foreign gods, and in the end even laid hands on God's Son and brought about eternal damnation. Moreover, every holy man is a loin cloth of God, who, taken from the earth and from the mud of the earth, is joined in the partnership of God, and covers and surrounds, with greater diligence, those things which appear obscene in His Church, so that they may not be exposed to the bites of the Gentiles and the heretics. And if this loin cloth touches water and crosses the streams of the Euphrates, so that it is soaked with the moisture of the Assyrian region, it loses its original strength and decays, and is dissolved. And although it returns to the use of God, it cannot have its former beauty, not due to the hardness of God, but due to its own fault: because they do not want to hear His words, and they walk in the wickedness of their own heart, doing what seems right to them. But He Himself explains why He has put forth this similitude, saying: Just as the girdle clings to the loins of a man: so I have joined and made to cling to Me the whole house of Israel, and the whole house of Judah, specifically the twelve tribes, so that they would be for Me a people renowned and for praise and for glory; and for all this, they did not listen to Me, but followed their own faults. Therefore, let the one who can say: 'But for me it is good to be close to God' (Psalm 73:28), beware lest he be separated from his reins through negligence and cross the Euphrates and be given into the power of the Assyrian king, and be occupied not in the most solid rock but in the crevice of a corrupted and tainted rock, that is, be occupied with the filth and vices of heretics, and come to such putrefaction that he can no longer return to the service and the belt of the Lord.
LETTER 40.1

Yet such is the order of nature. While truth is always bitter, pleasantness waits upon evildoing. Isaiah goes naked without blushing, as a type of the captivity to come. Jeremiah is sent from Jerusalem to the Euphrates (a river in Mesopotamia) and leaves his girdle to be marred in the Chaldaean camp, among the Assyrians hostile to his people. Ezekiel is told to eat bread made of mingled seeds and baked over the dung of people and cattle. He is commanded to experience the death of his wife without shedding a tear. Amos is driven from Samaria. Why is he driven from it? Surely in this case, as in the others, because he was a spiritual surgeon who cut away the parts diseased by sin and urged people to repentance. The apostle Paul says, "Am I therefore become your enemy because I tell you the truth?" And so the Savior found it, from whom many of the disciples turned back from following him because his sayings seemed hard.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 12

What the prophet is commanded by God to say ought to be worthy of God, [yet] it appears that it is not worthy of God so long as we remain at the level of the letter, so that someone else, on hearing the letter, might say: "These letters are folly." But it is the unspiritual man (psychikos) who will say this; for "the unspiritual man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him." Look, then, at what the wording says: "And you shall say to this people: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel" — what "the Lord, the God of Israel" says, let it be worthy of the Lord, the God of Israel — "Every wineskin shall be filled with wine. And it shall be, if they say to you: Do we not surely know that every wineskin shall be filled with wine?" And those who answer, if they take their stand on the literal statement and say these things, claiming to have known that "every wineskin shall be filled with wine," are lying. For it is not the case that "every wineskin shall be filled with wine." There are, at any rate, wineskins filled with oil or with some other liquid substance, and some even remain empty. They lie, then; for not every wineskin shall be filled with wine. And the people answer, saying: "Do we not surely know that every wineskin shall be filled with wine?" These words will receive from us, as far as we are able, an interpretation of the following sort. If we know the differences among wines and the things said about them, then in consequence we shall see, concerning the wineskins, that it is true that "every wineskin shall be filled with wine." For whether someone is a good wineskin, so to name it, among wineskins, it shall be filled with wine according to its own goodness; or whether, in comparison with wineskins and in the judgment concerning them, it is a wretched one, it too according to its wretchedness shall be filled with wretched wine. How, then, is it possible to gather from Scripture concerning the different wines? Concerning the worse ones this is written: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, a cluster of bitterness to them; their wine is the wrath of dragons, and the incurable wrath of asps." But concerning the better ones: "Your cup that inebriates me, how excellent it is," and Wisdom summons to her own bowl, saying: "Come, eat my bread, and drink wine which I have mingled for you." There is, then, a wine from Sodom, and there is a wine which Wisdom mixes. And again: "A vineyard came to be for the beloved on a horn, in a fertile place," planted by God, the vine called Sorek, which is a certain Chosen and Wondrous one. And there is also a certain vine of the Egyptians, which God strikes according to what is written: "God struck their vine with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost."

Consider for me, then, that all human beings are now, figuratively, capable of holding wine. And I name them for this reason wineskins, and I say that the base man is filled "with wine of the vine of Sodom," is filled with Egyptian wine and with the wine of the enemies of Israel, whereas the holy man who has been benefited is filled with wine from the vine Sorek and with the wine concerning which it is written: "Your cup that inebriates, how excellent it is," and again the holy man is filled with wine from that which Wisdom mixed. Let these things, then, be understood by me according to vice and virtue, so that the "every wineskin is filled with wine" may be contemplated. But if we must also see the things that come through vice and through virtue — punishments through vice, but blessings and promises through virtue — let us demonstrate from the sacred writings in what manner the punishments and the promises are called wine: "Take the cup of this unmixed wine, and you shall give all the nations to drink, to whom I shall send you." Jeremiah says these things; to which he adds: "And they shall drink and vomit and go mad and fall." So then he named the punishments here unmixed wine, which those drink who are worthy of unmixed wine, that is, of unmixed punishment. But there are also others who drink a punishment that is not unmixed, but mingled; for "a cup in the Lord's hand, full of unmixed wine of mingling, he inclined from this to that; yet its dregs were not emptied out; all the sinners of the earth shall drink." And if you wish also to see a cup of blessing, which the righteous drink, that of Wisdom would indeed have sufficed, in which she said: "Drink wine which I have mingled for you"; but behold for me also the Savior going up for the Passover into "a large upper room, furnished and adorned," and keeping the feast with his disciples and giving them a cup, concerning which it is written not that he mingled it; for Jesus, gladdening his disciples, gladdens them with unmixed wine, and says to them: "Take, drink, this is my blood, which is poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me," and: "Amen I say to you, I shall not drink it from now on, until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God."

Do you see the promise, which is "the cup of the new covenant"? Do you see the punishments as a cup of unmixed wine, and another kind of punishment as a mingled cup — so that it is mixed for each according to the worth of good action mingled with wretched action, which they will drink? Understand for me, on the one hand, those who are wholly alien to piety toward God and give no heed to themselves at all, but live at random, as drinking the unmixed wine concerning which we set forth the words from Jeremiah; but on the other hand, those who have not wholly fallen away, and yet are sinners — but unworthy of the cup "of the new covenant," doing at one time more upright, at another time contrary actions — as drinking wine "of unmixed mingling." For God "inclined from this to that." Of what "this"? I behold two cups, according to what is said: "He inclined from this to that; yet its dregs were not emptied out." Understand for me the cup of your good works in the one hand of God; but if you wish me to speak more boldly, let there be in the right hand of God the cup of your good works, and then let there be your cup of sins in the left hand of God. So then, when you are about to be punished for your sins — since more upright works too have come from you — "there is in the Lord's hand a cup of unmixed wine, full of mingling. And he inclined from this to that," from that in the left hand to that in the right. For neither can you drink only the cup of good things, as one who has not done only good works, nor can you drink only the cup of sins, for some upright things have been done by you. For this reason "he inclined from this to that." According to the proportion of your works, the wrath and the punishment are mixed for you, so that the punishment may be either more watery for you or sharper and more painful. For according to the proportion, as I said before, of the sins compared with the good deeds, that which is given from the cup of wrath is somehow blunted or is not blunted, a certain amount being given for each of the sins. But if you are wholly good and virtuous, you say: "I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord." "Every wineskin," then, whether good or wretched, "shall be filled with wine," and according to the fitness of the wineskin wine shall be cast into the wineskin, according to the account of the wineskins named here. Oil, then, is not put into the wineskins, nor any other liquid matter, but every wineskin must be filled with wine.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 30:5

And these things He said, setting laws and rules for His own disciples, that when they should have to receive as disciples those of all sorts that should come from the whole world, they might deal with them very gently. "Neither do men put new wine into old bottles." Seest thou His illustrations, how like the Old Testament? the garment? the wine skins? For Jeremiah too calls the people "a girdle," and makes mention again of "bottles" and of "wine." Thus, the discourse being about gluttony and a table, He takes His illustrations from the same.
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 12 onwards) You shall say therefore to them (or to the people) this message. Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Every pitcher (or vessel) shall be filled with wine. And they shall say to you: Do we not know that every pitcher (or vessel) shall be filled with wine? And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, and the kings who sit on David's throne, and the priests and the prophets and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. And I will scatter them, man from his brother, and fathers and sons together, says the Lord. I will not spare (or show mercy) and I will not relent, nor will I have compassion, so as not to destroy them. The Hebrew word Nebel () has been translated by the Aquila's first edition as 'laguncula', by the second edition as 'nebel' itself, by Symmachus as 'crater', by the LXX as 'utres', and by Theodotion as 'vas'. All of them interpret it as a vessel that is not filled with oil, water, honey, milk, or any other liquid material, but with wine and drunkenness. This shows that we are fragile vessels, as the Apostle says: 'But we have this treasure in earthen vessels' (2 Corinthians 4:7), and that it is impossible for us not to be filled with what is written: 'For no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh'. And again, I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that is what I practice (Rom. VII, 18). And then, wretched man that I am, who will rescue me from this body of death (Ibid., 19)? But by this drunkenness, where we forget the commandments of God, and every human condition is filled with vice and sin, as the Prophet says: No living being will be justified in your sight (Psal. CXLII, 2), not in comparison to God (as the ancient and new heretics claim, and the supporters of heretics), but in knowledge of Him: for man sees the face, but God sees the heart (I Sam. XVI, 7); and what may appear clean to us, is found filthy in His eyes: not only the common and lowly crowd, but also the kings of the Church, descendants or sons of David, who lie back with their heads raised and stretch their necks, and with outstretched necks, sit upon His throne. The priests themselves, the second in rank in ecclesiastical honor, and the prophets, who are thought to have knowledge of the Scriptures, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, are filled with a variety of sins: whether Jewish, as the Seventy have added. And when they are drunk, they are scattered from the company of their own, and fathers are separated from sons and sons from fathers, so that they are polluted by various heresies, and under the name of Christ they fight among themselves, and they fight against their mother, who gave birth to them, the Church. Where it says: I will not desire them, but I will have them in everlasting hatred: I will not spare, and I will not grant mercy, nor will I show compassion: not out of cruelty of judgment, but out of the truth of justice. For those who have slain my people, they themselves shall perish forever. This can be understood simply according to history, that kings, priests, and prophets, and all the people of Jerusalem must be made drunk with the cup of Babylon, and overwhelmed by the evils of captivity.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 12

Then he teaches, on account of those who had sinned — as far as the literal sense goes — in Jerusalem at that time and in Judea, with what sort of wine God is about to fill these wineskins, the sinners. For it is written: "If they say to you: Do we not surely know that every wineskin shall be filled with wine? then you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I fill all the inhabitants of this land, and the kings who sit as sons of David upon his throne, and the priests." He who is about to punish spares no one. Not because someone bore the title of prophet, yet has sins, will he not be filled with the threats that are spoken. Not because someone bore the title of priest and seemed to hold the preeminence of a more honorable name among the people does God spare him, so that he should not be punished when he has sinned. But the things recorded concerning those people, the apostle says, were written for our sake, "upon whom the ends of the ages have come." If, then, anyone even among these priests (and I point to us, the presbyters), or among these Levites who surround the people (I mean the deacons), sins, he will have this punishment; just as, again, there are certain priestly blessings, concerning which, God granting it, not far off but after the examination of the prophetic word, we shall learn when Numbers is read; for concerning priests certain things are about to be said there.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 12

"And the priests," then, "and the prophets and Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem" God says he will fill "with drunkenness" and will scatter "them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons." And let us understand these things also thus: the righteous God gathers together, but the sinners he scatters. For this reason, at the time when men did not move from the east, God did not scatter them; but when they moved "from the east" and "a man said to his neighbor: Come, and let us build for ourselves a city and a tower, whose top shall be up to heaven," God says concerning these: "Come, and going down let us confound their language there," and each one is confounded and is scattered to some place of the earth. And the people of Israel too, so long as they did not sin, were in Judea, but when they sinned they are scattered thereafter from the inhabited world and dispersed everywhere.

Understand something of this sort for me concerning all of us as well. There is a certain church of the firstborn who are enrolled in the heavens, where is Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. The blessed will be gathered together there, so that they may be together. But in this very thing the sinners are punished, in not being with one another. I know of some in this life who, for the sake of punishment, wish to hand over to some island, and for the sake of torment scatter the household of one who has offended the kingdom — the wife here, one son here, then the other elsewhere — so that not even in their misfortune may the mother enjoy the company of the son, or the brother of the brother. Understand something of this sort also in the case of the unjust. It is necessary that you, the sinner, taste something more bitter, being managed by God, so that being disciplined you may be saved. And just as you punish the household servant or son who is punished by you, not simply wishing to torture him, but that you may turn him back by the sufferings, so also God will discipline with the sufferings that come from afflictions those who do not turn back at the word, who have not been healed. He casts about, for the sake of discipline, the things he casts about, according to what is said: "Continually with suffering and scourge you shall be disciplined, Jerusalem." So then, in order that the disciplining suffering may increase, those who suffer are scattered from one another, so that this one and that one may not be together. For the intensity of the suffering would be relaxed through the consolation of each one toward the other.

But if we must add to the discussion yet another cause of the scattering, this too I shall set forth. Wicked men, being together with one another, contemplate evils and increase them, just as good men, being together with the good, deliberate about good things. [And] therefore the evil counsel is dissolved and divided — which would have prevailed with those like it — when the wretched are scattered from one another. For this reason God arranges that the base should not be with one another, perhaps even taking forethought for them, so that their wickedness may not grow together, but may be diminished by being dissolved. These things because of the "I will scatter them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons together. Says the Lord."

"I will not long for them, and I will not spare, and I will not have pity, from their destruction."

Those from the heresies pounce upon such literal statements, saying: Do you see what sort the Demiurge is? The God of the prophets, who says: "I will not spare and I will not have pity, from their destruction"? How can this one be good? But if I take as an example the judge who, for the sake of the common good, does not have pity, and the magistrate who rightly does not show mercy, I shall be able from the example to persuade that God, in sparing many, does not spare one. And I shall take as an example also a physician, showing that in sparing the whole body he does not spare one member. For instance, let this be set before a judge: to fashion peace and to prepare what is advantageous for the nation under him. And let there come forward some murderer brought to trial, fair in appearance and beautiful to behold. Let a mother come forward, offering pitiful words to the judge, so that her old age may be pitied; let the wife of this man who is unworthy to be pitied plead; let children standing around him beg on his behalf. In these circumstances, what is advantageous for the community? Is it that this man be pitied, or that he not be pitied? But if he is pitied, he will return to the same deeds; whereas if he is not pitied, he himself will die, but the community will be improved. So too God, if he spares the sinner and pities him and has compassion so as not to punish him — who will not be made worse? Which of the base, who cease from their sins even because of the fears of the places of punishment, will not be made worse, will not become worse? Such things can be seen happening in the churches too. Someone sinned, and after the sin he asked for communion. If he is too quickly pitied, the community is worn down. The sin of others grows. But if, by reasoning — not as one unmerciful nor as one savage is the judge, but as one taking forethought even for the one, and yet taking more forethought for the many than for the one — he considers the harm that will come to the community from the communion of the one and from the pardon of his sin, it is clear that he will cause the one to be cast out, so that he may save the many.

Behold for me also a physician, in what manner, if he is sparing about cutting what must be cut, if he is sparing about cauterizing what must be cauterized because of the pains that follow upon such remedies, in what manner the disease increases and becomes worse. But if he approaches the cutting and the burning somewhat more boldly, he will heal by not pitying, by seeming not to have compassion on the one who is cauterized and the one who is cut. So too God does not manage one man only, but manages the whole world, and administers everywhere the things in heaven and the things on earth. He considers, then, what is advantageous for the whole world and for all beings, and, as far as possible, he considers also what is advantageous for the one — yet not so that the advantage of the one should come to the detriment of the world. For this reason eternal fire too has been prepared, for this reason gehenna also has been made ready, for this reason there is also a certain outer darkness, of which there is need not only because of the one being punished, but especially because of the community.

But if you wish to take Scripture as a witness that sinners are punished even for the instruction of others, even if these are at some time despaired of as regards healing, hear Solomon saying in the Proverbs: "When a pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become more shrewd." He did not say that the one being scourged himself will become more shrewd and more prudent because of the scourges, but he says that the fool is changed from folly to prudence because of the scourges applied to the pestilent man; for this is what is signified here by the name of "shrewdness." And the fool is changed through seeing others being scourged. So then the punishment of others is advantageous to us, if indeed we become worthy of salvation through others being punished. And as the transgression of Israel was of profit to the salvation of the nations, so the punishment of some will be of profit to the salvation of others. For this reason, being good, God says: "I will not spare and I will not have pity, from their destruction."
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 12

Now that the one section has been circumscribed, let us see also what the other teaches us: "Hear and give ear, and be not lifted up, for the Lord has spoken. Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble upon dark mountains; and you will wait for light, and there will be a shadow of death there, and they will be set in darkness. But if you do not hear secretly, your soul will weep before the face of insolence, and your eyes will bring down tears, because the flock of the Lord has been crushed." He wishes these same people to hear and to give ear, being satisfied neither with their merely hearing nor with their merely giving ear. Therefore he says: "Hear and give ear." Then, after this, he commands them not to be lifted up, and teaches what must be done. What, then, is "to hear" and what is "to give ear," let us consider from the very wording. The "give ear" is "receive into the ears," and the "hear," if it is said in contradistinction to the "give ear," perhaps is "receive into the understanding." And among the things said in the Scriptures, some are more secret and more mystical, but others are useful straightaway to those who understand. Concerning the more secret things, I think, the "hear" is said, but concerning the things that are useful straightaway and able to benefit the hearer without interpretation, the "give ear"; if, then, we examine the whole of Scripture, we shall say, "having become approved money-changers": this, on the one hand, hear; this, on the other hand, give ear to.

Then, when we have heard and given ear, he commands us: "And be not lifted up." For "everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled." And the Savior too, in saying: "Learn from me, that I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls," teaches us not to be lifted up. For along with the other human evils, this sin too is much in us — at one time when we are lifted up quite unreasonably, and over that for which one ought not to be lifted up even to any degree, but at another time with plausibility, because that over which we are lifted up is reasonable, and yet the being lifted up even over that is not sound.

What I mean will be clear thus: there are some who are lifted up because they are sons of governors and because they are of a family among those of great worldly dignities. Such men, being lifted up over a matter that lies outside their choice and is indifferent, do not have even a reasonable plausibility that is brought forward to lead them toward being lifted up. There are those who are lifted up because they have authority to put men to death, and lifted up because they have received among themselves the advancement, so called, of such a kind as to cut off the heads of men. "The glory" of such men "is in their shame." Others are lifted up over wealth — not the true wealth but the lower — and others are lifted up, for example, over having a fine house or many fields. None of these things is worthy of account; one ought not to be lifted up over any of these.

But the plausible occasion for being lifted up is when someone is lifted up because he is wise, and is lifted up conscious to himself that already from the age of ten he has not touched sexual pleasures, or even from boyhood has not touched them; and again another is lifted up because he has worn bonds for Christ's sake. There is here a plausibility suggesting that one is reasonably lifted up; yet not even over these things, as regards the true reckoning, is one reasonably lifted up. Thus it is not reasonable to be lifted up even over these things. Paul had the material for being lifted up on account of the visions, on account of the sights, on account of the wonders and signs, on account of the labors which he labored for Christ, on account of the churches which he founded, being ambitious, where Christ had not been named, to lay the foundation of a church. All these were material for him — if one must speak with the plausibility concerning being lifted up — so that it might have seemed to some that he was rightly lifted up. But nevertheless, since not even the being lifted up over such things is without danger, the good Father, as he had granted him visions and sights, so also gave him, in the portion of a gift of grace, "an angel of Satan, to buffet him, so that he should not be over-exalted." And concerning this he besought the Lord three times, that "the angel of Satan," who had been given to him precisely so that he should not be lifted up, might depart from him. And the Lord answered him (for Paul was worthy of an answer from the Lord) and said to him: "My grace is sufficient for you; for my power is perfected in weakness." Over nothing, then, ought one to be lifted up; for falling follows upon being lifted up, according to the "before crushing the heart of a man is exalted, and before glory it is humbled." Let these things suffice for the "Hear and give ear, and be not lifted up, for the Lord has spoken."
Commentary on Jeremiah

(Verse 15.) Hear and perceive with your ears: Do not be lifted up, because the Lord has spoken. Because he said above, every vessel shall be filled with wine: so that even kings, and priests, and prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem may be filled with drunkenness, therefore he joins and says: Hear and perceive with your ears, both externally and internally, both in mind and body; and do not be lifted up with pride, considering your own weakness, and that there is no one who is without this drunkenness according to the extent of their sin. Where he is scattered, and corrupted, and unworthy of God's mercy, lifting himself up against Him through pride.
HOMILIES ON JEREMIAH 12

And let us see also what he bids us do after these things: "Give," he says, "to the Lord our God glory before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon dark mountains; and you will wait for light." He wishes the one who gives "glory to God" to give "glory to God" while there is light, since the glory of God cannot be proclaimed once it has grown dark and darkness has come. When, then, does it grow dark, and when does the darkening not occur? "Work while the light is in you." "The light is in" you if you have in you the one who said: "I am the light of the world." As long as this rises for you, glorify God; but know that a certain darkening can occur, and one must not let this darkening remain, but must give glory to God before it grows dark.

Perhaps we shall understand what is written by using an evangelical saying spoken by the Savior which runs thus: "Work while it is day; night comes when no one is able to work." He named there this present age "day" (but I necessarily added the "there"; for I know that in other places other things again are indicated) — he named, then, this present age "day," but darkness and night the consummation, because of the punishments. For "why do you desire the day of the Lord? And this is darkness and not light," says the prophet Amos. If you see what the gloom is after the consummation of the world, that which follows when almost the whole race of men is punished for the things they have sinned, you will see that then that which surrounds has grown dark, and no one any longer is able to glorify God, seeing that the word of God commanded even the righteous, saying: "Go, my people, enter into your chamber, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while, until the wrath of my anger pass by." And at the same time, in these words, let anyone who is able observe that he said: "a little while." But that "little while" is little for God; it is not little for a man; for one must see that for each thing there is something little and something great. And from an example I shall demonstrate that for each thing there is something little or great. For every animal such-and-such an amount of food is little in comparison with its constitution, and such-and-such an amount of food is much again in comparison with its constitution. And thus what is little for a man is great for another animal. What is little, for example, for a man is much for a child. Thus the whole time of human life is little, even the time of the long-lived man, in comparison with the whole of the entire present age. So indeed the "little" of God is much in comparison with us, and a whole age is the "little" of God. If, then, it is said: "Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while," that "little" must be thought to be spoken not in relation to the condition of the one commanded to go and to enter into his chambers, but in relation to the condition of the one who commands these things, for whom that which is much for this man is little. For if, "until the wrath of the anger" of God "pass by," some must enter into their chambers, and there are those for whom "the sins are not forgiven, not only throughout this whole age but also throughout the whole age to come," it is clear that the "little" is extended alongside the things that have been said.

"Give," therefore, "glory to the Lord our God." How do we give glory to the Lord our God? It is not in voices and little phrases that I seek the giving of glory to the Lord our God, but in deeds the one who gives glory to the Lord God gives glory to him. Glorify God in self-control (sōphrosynē), in righteousness, in doing good glorify God; give glory to God in courage and endurance, give glory to God in piety and holiness and the remaining virtues. And if these things are so, and one glorifies God in this way, then if I state the opposite, do not think that I am blaspheming; for I will bring forward the Scripture as a witness of those things too. The self-controlled man glorifies God, the one who lives licentiously dishonors God. For, like Nebuchadnezzar, he overturns the temple of God and "corrupts the temple of God" and "through the transgression of the law dishonors God" (this too is an apostolic expression). The sinner, then, clothes God with dishonor. And questions are raised concerning providence, so that some doubt whether providence exists; but providence is nothing other than [what is questioned] on account of evil. Take away the evil, and you do not stumble against providence. But up and down those who stumble against providence say these things: why are there so many adulterers and so many effeminate men, why are there so many godless and impious people? And it is the sinners who beget dishonor for providence, stumbling-blocks against God, blasphemy against the one who created the world. Some, then, do give glory to God, but they do not give glory to God who do the things opposite to the glory of God through their sins.

"Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains." There are certain dark mountains, there are certain luminous mountains; but since there are both. The luminous mountains are the holy angels of God, the prophets, Moses the servant, the apostles of Jesus Christ. All these are luminous mountains, and I think it is concerning these that it has been said in the Psalms: "His foundations are in the holy mountains." But what sort of mountains are dark? Those who raise up high things against the knowledge of God. The devil is a dark mountain; the rulers of this age who are being brought to nothing are dark mountains; and the demon, the epilepsy (moon-affliction), was a mountain, and it was a dark mountain, concerning which the Savior said: "You shall say to this mountain." For when the discussion concerned the epilepsy and the disciples said, "Why were we not able to cast it out?", the Savior answers that "if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain," concerning which you put forward the question, concerning which you inquired, "you shall say to this mountain: Move from here to there, and it shall move." "From here" — away from the man; "there" — to its own proper place. Those, then, who stumble do not stumble upon luminous mountains, but upon dark mountains, whenever they come to be with the devil and his angels, the dark mountains.

"And you shall wait for light." Now "and you shall wait for light" can be joined to "give glory to the Lord our God." If you give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon dark mountains," it is clear that, even if it does grow dark, "you shall wait for the light" and the light shall receive you in succession.
